children: By David Conti

At Fidelity, I used to joke with colleagues that people don't get truly serious about retirement planning until they have a health scare — or hit a milestone birthday, like 50. Now I realize that 60 is another milestone birthday. That's when people get a retirement-planning wake-up call.

These aren't people who failed to save. In many cases, they did almost everything right. They contributed to 401(k)s for decades, built IRAs and brokerage accounts, paid down the mortgage and accumulated substantial assets. Many are confident do-it-yourself investors.
Then retirement gets close enough to feel real, and they have an "Aha!" moment: "We have assets, but we don't have a plan."

At age 40 or 50, the big question is often: "Am I saving and investing enough?" At 60, the questions multiply. Can we maintain our lifestyle for another 30 years? When should we claim Social Security? Which accounts should we pull money from first? How will taxes change when the paycheck disappears? Can we help the kids or grandkids? What happens if one of us lives to 95 or longer?

For advisors, age 60 creates an opening with a group that can be hard to reach: smart, successful DIY investors who are beginning to realize that portfolio management is no longer the main issue and they need help with planning their retirement.

The question about having enough money to retire only scratches the surface, says Lisa Kirchenbauer, founder of Omega Wealth Management in Arlington, Va. "We look at the entire picture: insurance, estate planning, tax planning," she says.

Some clients initially hire Omega for a second opinion. They ask: Are we on track? Are we invested appropriately for retirement? Are we paying more in taxes than we need to? For clients who want to go deeper, the conversation changes to life planning and Omega asks clients: What are you retiring to? What do you want retirement to look like? How do you think about legacy?

Kirchenbauer points to one executive couple in healthcare who had accumulated a sizable portfolio, much of it at Vanguard, but had no comprehensive retirement plan. Her team worked through the planning basics, created a donor-advised fund, reviewed insurance and coordinated with the couple's CPA and estate-planning attorney.

Another Omega client arrived with roughly $10 million in assets after careers in healthcare and education. They had saved and invested well enough to consider retiring early, in their mid-50s. But wealth had created a new set of questions around taxes, legacy and family.
Blind spots. The challenge for advisors is that successful DIY investors may know their investments well while having had little exposure to financial planning.

Jeffrey L. Corliss, managing director at Hightower Signature Wealth in Westport, Conn., recently started working with a physician in Fairfield County with a portfolio of more than $10 million. The doctor and his spouse earn about $500,000 a year and expect to retire in a few years, when that earned income will drop to zero.

Corliss started with cash flow. The couple estimates they will need about $350,000 a year to support an active retirement. Their daughter and son-in-law had just moved to California, which raised an immediate planning question: Could they afford to buy a condo there?

"They realize at age 60 they have a lot of money, but don't have a comprehensive strategy," Corliss says. "What about healthcare? How much risk should they be taking at this life stage? Now that they have grandkids, how should that factor into their financial planning?"

The clues often come from listening closely. If a client mentions helping grandchildren and then looks across the table to a spouse for confirmation, Corliss sees useful information about how the couple makes money decisions. "We ask more questions, we listen, and we design the path they can move forward with," he says.

Mind the gaps. That process can uncover surprisingly basic gaps. For a newly retired multimillionaire, the financial blind spot may have little to do with security selection. For example, Corliss cites clients who update an estate plan but forget to retitle assets afterward.

Pam Krueger, founder of Wealthramp in Osterville, Mass., hears from investors every day who are nearing retirement and looking for fee-only advisors. She recently received an inquiry from a longtime DIY investor preparing to move from accumulation to drawdown.

The investor wanted help with retirement timing, withdrawal strategies, Roth conversions, Social Security, required minimum distributions, asset allocation, sequence-of-returns risk, tax planning and legacy planning.

The list itself tells the story. For decades, the portfolio had one primary job: grow. Now it has to help produce a retirement paycheck, absorb market shocks, fund taxes, support spending and perhaps leave money behind.

That shift can make even experienced investors decide they no longer want to manage everything themselves. Krueger says a planning-retainer relationship can be a useful entry point. "You don't want to marry your new advisor on the first date," she says. Some investors start with a retainer and deepen the relationship after 12 or 18 months.

That also gives the advisor time to demonstrate value beyond investment selection. "When the advisor shows they can aptly stress-test the client's worst fears, that builds a lot of confidence," says Krueger.

Why they wait. There may be a psychological reason successful DIY investors wait so long to ask for help. Tyler Rosier, a neuroscientist and author of Wired for Wealth, says professional success can reinforce the belief that financial complexity can be mastered the same way someone mastered a career.
But the skills don't transfer perfectly. "Stock-picking skills don't automatically translate to managing risks like sequence-of-return risk, which becomes critical near retirement," Rosier says.

Age and identity can complicate the transition further. "What is a strength in one season of life can become a weakness in another," he says. Long-term professional success can become part of someone's identity, making it harder to acknowledge that outside help may now be useful.

That matters for advisors trying to win over a new 60-year-old client. The job isn't to tell a successful investor everything they did wrong over the previous 30 years. It is to establish enough trust to deal with the decisions that can't be postponed: cash flow, healthcare, taxes, Social Security, estate planning, family support and portfolio risk.

The advisor may wish the client had made catch-up contributions at 50, funded an HSA more aggressively, or diversified a concentrated position years earlier. But the planning starts with the facts as they exist today.

Successful DIY investors got this far through discipline, curiosity, judgment and, yes, sometimes luck. The question is whether the same approach that built the portfolio is enough to carry a family through the next 25 or 30 years.
Bottom line. Advisors have an opportunity to attract new clients who are going through an age-60 awakening. That's when they realize, "We have assets. Now we need a plan."

David Conti, CPRC, is a New Hampshire-based retirement coach at RetireMentors, with over 20 years of experience in retirement planning. He spent 17 years in financial communications at Fidelity Investments, where he served as the personal finance and retirement editor for Fidelity Viewpoints.
